title: Leaders Who Overfish
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This piece borrows the ecological concept of overfishing to describe a leadership failure mode: sacrificing a team's long-term development for short-term convenience. The author identifies three specific, usually unintentional ways leaders 'overfish' — over-relying on top performers, funneling growth opportunities to people who don't need them, and pulling high performers away from mentoring duties. Each pattern trades a quick result for a depleted future talent pool, mirroring how overfishing depletes fish populations that can no longer replenish themselves.
points: Leaders 'overfish' by repeatedly leaning on the same top performers for hard tasks, burning them out while under-developing everyone else.
Giving growth-oriented assignments to already-strong performers instead of those who need the experience stunts the development of less-seasoned team members.
Pulling top performers away from coaching and mentoring duties to maximize short-term results eliminates a key channel of team-wide development.
Overfishing behaviors trade short-term results for a depleted, unsustainable long-term talent pipeline.
quotes: Overfishing occurs when so many fish are caught in a given population that there are not enough adults left to breed and sustain a healthy population of future fish.
Leaders can overfish in their teams in three primary ways, all of which are usually unintentional.
This depletes the energy of top performers and has the potential to burn them out.
Saving developmental experiences for those who need them most grows team skill.
They sacrifice long-term benefits of team member growth and development for short-term gains.
